Computing In The Time Of COVID
Amir Husain, Forbes, 2020-10-12

I can feel it. The COVID-19 pandemic has revitalized the desktop PC scene.

Prior to the stay-at-home regulations and lockdowns, we were merrily skipping about from coffee shops to juice bars, leaving our PCs behind and trying to do more on tiny mobile devices and small laptops. But we didn't get all this mobility for free. For our miniature devices, we paid outsized prices. We made do with a smaller amount of compute power, settled for reduced screen real estate, gave up true multitasking on our phones and improvised with tiny keyboards on which we hunted and pecked with our thumbs.

The amount of work we could do on our tiny mobile devices and half-inch thick laptops while on the go seemed so empowering. But now that we are at home, sitting in front of honest-to-goodness desks, we realize what we were missing. Multiple screens, large TVs driven by top of the line GPUs, fantastic full-size mechanical keyboards, high-resolution mice, full-blooded multi-core processors, wired GigE connections, real speakers and high quality subwoofers, terabytes of local storage and a farm of local servers and VMs on which to experiment. Perhaps that sounds like overkill to many, but please don't tell me you prefer a keyboard that measures three inches across, or a six-inch screen, to real peripherals made not for ants but for full-size humans—who are at least three times as big (please see: the gospel of Zoolander).

Now, it isn't all fun and games. This shift from "mobile first" to "biggest screen first" has certainly claimed its casualties. Jeffery Katzenberg, founder of heavily-funded short-form streaming platform, Quibi, believes that the coronavirus pandemic has essentially destroyed his company's business model. Quibi was intended to be a media company producing content for those moments of downtime we used to have at work, and was built around the premise that content would be watched on six-inch screens. In another confirmation of the fact that no one is interested in six-inch screens for content viewing when they can have better, Quibi is now up for sale. Venture Wire reports that the "sharks are circling."

It's not surprising that desktops are more efficient, but it’s kind of fascinating how far we went in shifting workflows to mobile devices in ye olde times, before the present apocalypse. I find that an email that takes five minutes to respond to on a mobile device takes only a minute on a desktop. A programming project on a desktop with multiple monitors and a real mechanical keyboard seems so much more enjoyable than on a laptop with keys that have hardly any travel, and real multitasking with multiple windows arranged on multiple monitors makes almost everything you do on computers better. My research here, my task list there, my email on that screen and my calendar on the other one. All visible at a glance.

We were saving time with mobile devices. But we were also wasting time, hunting and pecking when we could have touch typed our way to inbox zero. We were painfully moving from the browser window to the email application repeatedly, jotting down links, facts and references, when we could have both open side by side on a widescreen monitor.

Desktop computers are better at everything, aside from being mobile.

But wait, there's more!

Personally, I've transformed the lockdown into an opportunity (take that, COVID!) to go far beyond a "desk" top, in the sense of a computer residing on a single desk. I'm now to the point where essentially my entire office is a living computer. And I'm loving this "room as a computer" concept. Twenty-five USB3 ports across two powered hubs connect up Logitech video cameras, speakers, headphones, yeti microphones, a mechanical keyboard with God’s own Alps SKCM switches and a wired Razr mouse. Another mechanical bluetooth keyboard and wireless trackball provide alternative control from a sofa in the corner of the office. Three monitors and a fourth large-format Samsung TV—each connected to its own independent GPU—allow e-mailing, conference calls, media watching, programming, writing and research. Two Raspberry Pi’s live just behind the displays, connected to a deskarea switch. One runs a Plex media server, while the other runs RetroPi and is connected to one of the multi-input HDMI monitors, as well as to a wireless Logitech trackpad/keyboard combo and a wired game controller. A small adjustable stand mounts an iPad, which effectively serves as the fifth desk display. A Xeon server in the home data center, a backup storage box, a tiny ARM-based Linux server and a cluster of Intel-based Linux systems provide additional resources, including Jupyter, experimental web servers, NFS, CIFS and more.

Next to the desk, a small rack houses a growing army of Thinkpads (with real keyboards), organized in a vertical storage system. Below this are a number of ARM boards which accept remote connections, offering Linux development environments and IoT experimentation. A few travel phones also reside herein, ignored for months.

The rest of the home network now numbers 50+ active nodes. And I haven't even begun to talk about the retro computer collection! But that's a different story for another day. It embarrasses me to go on. And I’m not obsessive... you’re obsessive!

But in all seriousness, the point in all of this is not that I dislike mobile computers and phones. Quite the contrary, I love them. How else does one write while in the car on a long drive, if not on a laptop? Or jot down ideas that wake you up at 3:30 am, if not with the Drafts app on the bedside iPhone? Certain tools are more appropriate for certain jobs. And the pandemic has helped me recognize that I was often losing time by attempting to do things most suited for desktop computers on small mobile devices.

I've also realized that interacting with desktop computers actually brings out the content creator in me more so than a mobile device does. One of my pet peeves (ok, fine, my existential fear...) has been this idea that I will devolve into a content consumer, mindlessly accepting information put together by others, and not doing enough to produce or write meaningful things myself. I'm OK with using, but I delight in building. The desktop environment is just intrinsically more conducive to that type of creative role.

Finally, interactions with a desktop computer are an invitation to do things that you would not be able to do on mobile devices. They allow you to truly leverage "computation" and go beyond the mere short-form communication that mobile devices are good for. It is my long-held view that we haven't really discovered the power of computers yet. Computational leverage requires skill and a lot of imagination, so the last four decades of personal computing have all been about exploiting the low-hanging fruit of enabling human communication through computers. A great opportunity lies ahead in unlocking the computational abilities of personal computers.

Perhaps a creative developer will discover a path to that future while busily hacking away on Emacs running inside tmux (why? Emacs is a windowing OS that employs a variety of large bootloaders that most people think of as operating systems) on their Das Keyboard during the pandemic.

How have your interactions with computers changed in 2020? Do you find yourself sitting at a desk and using human-sized peripherals and multiple monitors? If so, do you feel your productivity has increased as a consequence? I would love to hear your thoughts about how your relationship with computing has changed over these last six months. Until then, I’ll be here at my honest-to-goodness desk enjoying the friendly glow of my giant displays. And those Alps switches... I tell ya!
